subject: feat(table): support geometry Hilbert-curve ordering for data file rewrites (#2517)
body:
Adds `WithCompactionGeometryHilbertOrder`, which orders each partition of a compaction group along a Hilbert curve over the centre of a top-level geometry or geography column's XY bounding box, so rows close in space share files and row groups and spatial filters prune more files. Refs #2043.

- `WithHilbertBits` sets grid resolution (default 16 bits per axis, max 32); `WithHilbertBounds` fixes the extent instead of deriving it from the data.
- Cannot be combined with `WithCompactionSortOrder`; rejects non-geo columns, out-of-range bits and bad bounds.
- Output files record no `sort_order_id`, since a Hilbert order is not an Iceberg sort order.
- Rows with a null or empty geometry go last; geography is ordered on planar x/y with no antimeridian wrapping; the whole group is held in memory.
- Gather and batching code is shared with the sort strategy with no change to the sort algorithm.

This is not Java's multi-column `hilbert(c1, c2)` sort order (apache/iceberg#16827), which encodes primitive columns and does not accept geometry; the plain `WithCompactionHilbertOrder` name is left free for a Java-compatible option.

subject: fix(table): check partial-progress batches against the planning snapshot (#2302)
body:
* fix(table): check partial-progress batches against the planning snapshot

Partial-progress compaction plans every group once, then commits batches one by one, each starting from the previous batch's committed table. When a batch's refresh-and-replay retry rebases onto a peer snapshot, that snapshot becomes the next batch's base, so the next batch's commit-time validator never sees it. If the peer added a position delete or deletion vector for a data file in a later batch, that batch rewrote the file from tasks planned without the delete, then CollectDeadPositionDeletes removed the delete as dead, bringing the deleted rows back.

Before rewriting a batch, run the rewrite conflict rules over every snapshot committed since planning. A conflicting batch is recorded in FailedGroups and counts toward MaxFailedCommits, like a failed commit, and nothing is written for it.

* test(table): pin rejected batches against MaxFailedCommits

Address review: count planning-snapshot rejections toward
MaxFailedCommits in a test, and update the FailedGroups doc to cover
batches rejected before reaching the catalog. Rebase onto main
(AddFiles is now AddDataFilesByPath).

* refactor(table): read each snapshot once when checking partial-progress batches

Collect the delete files committed since planning incrementally, so each
batch only reads snapshots committed since the previous batch instead of
rewalking the whole window. Document that partial-progress groups must be
planned from the transaction's table, and report batches rejected by the
planning check as rejected rather than committed.

* test(table): cover deletion vectors absorbed by an earlier partial-progress batch

subject: fix(table): use one transaction replay path and renew snapshot timestamps (#2468)
body:
* fix(table): replay every retried transaction through stagedReplay

`Transaction.Commit` created `stagedReplay` only for transactions with snapshot expiry. Other retries used `rebuildSnapshotUpdates`, which ignored staged ref moves. After a peer committed to another branch, a retry could undo `RollbackToSnapshot` by rebuilding the following append on the head from before the rollback. A ref reset between two appends could also give the second append the wrong parent.

Use `stagedReplay` for every refreshed attempt and remove `rebuildSnapshotUpdates`. `Transaction.Commit` supplies replay state, and `doCommit` creates it when none is supplied. `stagedReplay.requirements` supplies expiry assertions for each attempt.

If a staged update cannot apply after refresh, return `ErrTransactionUnusable` for every transaction. Preserve the metadata builder's cause, including `ErrCommitFailed` for conflicts. A catalog rejection on the first attempt still returns `ErrCommitRejected` and leaves the transaction resumable. A later `Commit` refreshes and replays, and ends the transaction if the update cannot apply.

Signed-off-by: Harrison Crosse <harrison@crosse.dev>

* fix(table): renew snapshot timestamps when replaying a retry

A retry kept each staged snapshot's original timestamp, whether it rebuilt or reused the manifest list. If a peer wrote metadata more than a minute after staging, the metadata builder rejected the snapshot and ended the transaction. Replaying every transaction locally also exposed this rejection for REST catalogs. A server using Java's `TableMetadata` could accept this retry on a branch other than `main`, or when the peer added no entry to the snapshot log for `main`.

Stamp each replayed producer snapshot with the current time, or one millisecond after its parent if that is later. This follows Java's `SnapshotProducer` timestamp rule. The manifest list, summary and IDs do not carry the timestamp, so renewal changes only the snapshot's timestamp and metadata derived from it.

The committed timestamp reflects the successful attempt rather than staging time. If `ExpireSnapshots` was staged after the write in the same transaction, retry replanning keeps the renewed snapshot because it is newer than the expiry cutoff. Java instead expires the snapshot selected on its first attempt.

Signed-off-by: Harrison Crosse <harrison@crosse.dev>

subject: feat(table): sort-order rewrite strategy for data file compaction (#2345)
body:
* feat(table): add sort-order data file compaction

Compaction only bin-packed: ExecuteCompactionGroup streamed each
group's rows straight into WriteRecords, which sorts every record batch
on its own by the table's default sort order. Output files were
therefore sorted per batch, not per file, overlapped each other on the
sort key, and recorded no sort_order_id.

WithCompactionSortOrder switches a group rewrite to sort. The group's
rows are materialized, split by the table's current partition spec,
and each partition is sorted as a whole with sort_indices. Sorted rows
are gathered from the source batches one output batch at a time, so no
column is concatenated beyond one output batch (Arrow's chunked Take
would concatenate whole struct, list and decimal columns per call).
The writer is told the stream is presorted: it skips the per-batch
sort, and since every rolled file is a contiguous run of the stream,
each file records the order's id as sort_order_id when the order is
one of the table's sort orders and every field is a single-source,
order-preserving transform.

Splitting by partition before sorting keeps the stream clustered for
the clustered writer even when a group spans files written under an
older partition spec.

compaction.Config.RewriteAll mirrors Java's rewrite-all so files that
size-based selection skips as optimal can be sorted too. The CLI gains
`compact run --sort` (table default sort order) and `--rewrite-all`.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>
Signed-off-by: saurabhojha <ojhasaurabh2099@gmail.com>

* feat(table): k-way merge presorted files in sort compaction

When every file of a sort group records the order's sort_order_id and
was written under the current partition spec, ExecuteCompactionGroup
now reads each file as its own stream and k-way merges the streams per
partition instead of materializing and sorting the whole group. Memory
drops from the decoded group to about two batches per file. Each merge
step copies the longest run of the minimum stream that precedes the
runner-up as one zero-copy slice, so files with disjoint ranges are
merged a batch at a time. A file whose rows are not actually sorted
fails the group rather than producing output that claims an order it
does not have. Scan.readTasksPerTask backs the merge: one stream per
task sharing one set of delete loaders, so a shared position or
equality delete file is read once.

Sorting now uses one Iceberg-ordered row comparator for both the
in-memory sort and the merge. Arrow's sort kernel places NaN next to
nulls, while the spec puts NaN after +Inf ascending and first
descending. Bound to a partition's batches the comparator matches the
kernel's speed (1M rows: ~347ms vs ~345ms int64, ~548ms vs ~570ms
string).

sort_order_id is now claimed only when every field but the last is
identity. Ordering by the source column of a coarser transform such as
day(ts) also orders the rows the transform ties on, so for
[day(ts), id] the rows were not sorted by id within a day.

* feat(compaction): cap groups by MaxGroupSizeBytes

PlanCompaction bin-packed each partition's candidates to
TargetFileSizeBytes, so a group held about one output file's worth of
input. That suits bin-pack, but a sort rewrite orders rows only within
a group: with one-file groups every sorted output file of a partition
overlapped the others on the sort key, and files from an earlier sort
rewrite (already target-sized) each landed in a group of their own, so
the k-way merge path never saw two of them together.

compaction.Config.MaxGroupSizeBytes, mirroring Java's
max-file-group-size-bytes, caps a group's input size independently of
the output file size; ExecuteCompactionGroup already rolls output at
the target size, so one group yields many sorted, non-overlapping
files. Zero keeps the previous packing, so existing plans are
unchanged. The CLI gains --max-group-size on compact analyze and run.

* fix(table): address sort compaction merge review

- Merge only orders whose fields are all identity. The merge compares
  source values, and a file sorted by [day(ts)] may validly be unsorted
  by ts within a day, so such files failed the group on every run. They
  now take the in-memory path; output still records the id when it is
  claimable.

  stream, so a partition with more files than the scan concurrency now
  takes the in-memory path instead of opening every file at once. Docs
  state the real cost: up to about five batches per merged file.

  give mostly one-row runs, and concatenating a slice per run made the
  merge ~20x slower than sorting in memory. Runs are now recorded as
  (batch, range) and each output batch is built with the existing Take
  gather; a batch that is one run stays a zero-copy slice. On 2 x 131k
  rows x 32 int64 columns: interleaved 1.32s -> 64ms, disjoint 3ms
  unchanged (BenchmarkMergeInterleaved/Disjoint).

  the in-memory path can reach about twice the group's decoded size and
  is always taken by the first sort rewrite.

subject: fix(table): make NotIn skip NULL rows in scans (#2369)

Why: the record filter compiled a multi-value NOT IN as not(is_in(x, set)),

scans for the multi-value form. Guard the negation with is_not_null so
NOT IN never matches NULL, whichever path built it.

subject: fix(table): treat stale snapshot values as commit conflicts (#2342)
body:
When a peer commits on another branch, the commit branch requirement
still holds, but the metadata builder rejects the staged snapshot
because its sequence number is no longer above last-sequence-number, or
on v3 its first-row-id is behind next-row-id. The SQL, Glue, Hive and
Hadoop catalogs returned that rejection as a plain error, so doCommit
treated it as an unknown commit state: it did not retry, skipped
cleanup, and Transaction.Commit refused a re-commit, although nothing
was written and a refresh and rebuild would land it.

Wrap ErrCommitFailed for these two checks only, as Java does with
RetryableValidationException, which its REST handlers report as a 409.
The row-id rejection still matches ErrInvalidRowLineage. The timestamp
checks and every other builder error stay unchanged, since a rebuild
keeps the snapshot timestamp and would fail the same way.

subject: fix(catalog/hive): keep the caller's view version in CreateView (#2353)
body:
Hive's CreateView only used the caller's version to pick a SQL string,
then rebuilt the view from that one representation. The stored metadata
lost the other representations and the caller's summary, default
namespace and default catalog, which was always written as "hive".
Java's BaseMetastoreViewCatalog keeps what the engine passes.

Add view.CreateViewFromVersion, which writes the caller's version as is
apart from its IDs, and use it from Hive. CreateView and
CreateViewWithIOProperties now delegate to it, and the SQL catalog can
reuse it once its view API matches ViewCatalog. The metastore's view
text still comes from the Hive-dialect SQL.

Refs #2062

subject: fix(table): delete manifests that superseded commit attempts wrote (#2343)
body:
Merge-append and overwrite rebuild their manifests against the fresh
parent on every retry and every resumed Commit. A merge writes new
merged manifests, and an overwrite writes rewritten parent manifests
and tombstones. doCommit tracked only the manifest lists those passes
wrote, so a retried commit that landed left attempt 0's manifests and
every superseded rebuild's manifests unreferenced on storage, and a
failed commit left the manifests its rebuilds wrote.

Every snapshot producer now records the manifests each pass writes,
replacing the rewrite producer's private superseded list, and doCommit
treats them like manifest lists. Once a commit lands it deletes the
recorded manifests no committed snapshot references, including attempt
0's. After a known failure it deletes only those this call's rebuilds
wrote, and after an unknown commit state it deletes nothing. Before
deleting, it reads every committed snapshot's manifest list and keeps
the files they reference.

A merge that consumes its added-content manifest now deletes it once
the commit lands, with or without a retry, as Java's
MergingSnapshotProducer does. The rewrite producer still keeps its
merged manifests after a failed commit, since a resume can reuse them.

subject: feat(table): convert equality deletes to deletion vectors (#2434)
body:
**What**
- Convert v3 equality deletes to file-specific deletion vectors.

**Why**
- Reduce repeated equality-delete work in later CDC scans.

**Implementation**
- Read each data file targeted by an applicable equality delete.
- Commit the conversion in one replace snapshot.
- Reject conversion when an unscoped or partition-scoped position delete would remain.
- Reject concurrent first DVs in merge-on-read `DELETE` with `ErrConflictingDeleteFiles`.
- A concurrent branch commit may fail with `ErrCommitFailed`; refresh and retry.
- Abandoned staged transactions may leave Puffin files for orphan cleanup.

**Benchmark**
- Same synthetic local scan: one 10k-row file with 10% deletes: upstream/main 2.062 ms / 3.10 MB; branch 1.648 ms / 2.81 MB (median of 3 runs).

**References**
- Java [BaseDVFileWriter](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/main/core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/deletes/BaseDVFileWriter.java) and [DeleteFile](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/main/api/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/DeleteFile.java).
- Iceberg spec: [Deletion Vectors](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#deletion-vectors) and [Equality Delete Files](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#equality-delete-files).

subject: fix(table): reject AddColumn when the column name already exists (#2626)
body:
UpdateSchema.AddColumn only failed for an existing name when a pending
update in the same struct had that name. Otherwise it added a second
column with the same name: Apply returned a schema with duplicate names,
Commit failed with a visitor error, and in case-insensitive mode a
column that only differs in case was committed. A name that another
column is renamed to in the same update was not checked at all.

AddColumn and UnionByNameWith now reject a name that an existing column
keeps, that another column is renamed to, or that an earlier add used,
comparing names with the update's case sensitivity. As in Java's
SchemaUpdate and PyIceberg's UpdateSchema, a deleted column's name can
still be reused. A column renamed to another name also gives up its
name, as before.

subject: fix(table): reject deleting an identifier column (#2523)
body:
* fix(table): reject deleting an identifier column

UpdateSchema.DeleteColumn removed the deleted column from the identifier
field names, so deleting an identifier column silently dropped it from
the table's identifier fields. Deleting the struct that contains an
identifier field, or the same column with different case in
case-insensitive mode, already failed in Apply.

Keep the identifier field names unchanged on delete, so Apply rejects
the deleted identifier field unless SetIdentifierField replaces the
identifier fields, as Java's SchemaUpdate and PyIceberg's UpdateSchema
do.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Shivam Sharma <192242476+ShivamSharma43@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(table): check deleted identifier fields against the original schema

As Java's SchemaUpdate does, Apply now looks up each identifier field in
the original schema and rejects it if that field, or a struct containing
it, is being deleted. The error now says the identifier field is being
deleted instead of "identifier field not found", and deleting an
identifier column and adding a new column with the same name no longer
moves the identifier to the new field. A renamed identifier is not in
the original schema under its new name, so it skips this check.

Add a compatibility note for the behaviour change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Shivam Sharma <192242476+ShivamSharma43@users.noreply.github.com>

subject: feat(table)!: retry conflicting commits 4 times by default (#2462)
body:
commit.retry.num-retries has defaulted to 0 since #912, when a retry
re-sent the same stale commit. #945 added refresh-and-replay, so that
reason is gone, and Java and PyIceberg both default to 4. A writer
ported from either client, or sharing a table with them, failed on the
first conflict with nothing in the code pointing at retries.

The default is now 4, and the docs and a compatibility note say so.
Setting commit.retry.num-retries to 0 keeps the old fail-fast behavior.
Tests that exercise the no-retry and resume paths now set it explicitly,
and a new test checks that a conflict is retried within one Commit by
default.

Closes #1015.
Refs #2062.

subject: fix(table): write statistics blob metadata Java can read (#2358)
body:
* fix(table): write statistics blob metadata Java can read

A statistics blob with no properties was written as "properties": null,
and one with no fields as "fields": null, in table metadata and
set-statistics updates. Iceberg Java 1.12 rejects both in
TableMetadataParser and MetadataUpdateParser, so the whole metadata load
fails. Metadata Java wrote hit it too: Java omits empty properties, Go
decoded that to a nil map, and the next Go write emitted null.

Omit empty properties and write nil fields as [], which is what Java
writes for the same blobs.

* fix(table): write empty statistics blob metadata as []

A StatisticsFile with no blobs was written as "blob-metadata": null,
which Java's StatisticsFileParser rejects.

subject: fix(view): reuse existing versions from base metadata (#2470)
body:
Replacing a view with a definition it already had (for example,
reverting to an earlier query) failed with "duplicate version-id".
addVersion found the matching version and reused its ID, but only
skipped the append if the version had been added in the current
builder. Versions from the base metadata were appended again.

Return the existing version ID whenever the version is already known,
as Java's ViewMetadata.Builder.addVersionInternal does. The last added
version ID is only set when the version was added in this builder.

subject: refactor!: remove VisitBoundPredicateRef from the public API (#2623)
body:
VisitBoundPredicateRef was exported and gated only by an
internal.BoundPredicateRef parameter. A caller in another module could
still reach it, because generic type inference lets it pass the zero
value of a type it cannot name. That handed borrowed literal sets, and
the precomputed IN extrema, to visitors outside iceberg-go.

Remove the function and move the zero-copy dispatch into
VisitBoundPredicate. A visitor gets the predicate's own sets, and
VisitInWithExtrema, only when it has a BorrowBoundSets method whose
parameter is internal.BoundPredicateRef. Code outside the module cannot
name that type, so it cannot declare the method.

The four evaluators in table/evaluators.go gain the marker. They are
unexported and not returned by any exported API, so outside code cannot
embed them to inherit it.

subject: test(catalog/sql): encode warehouse paths as file URIs in namespace tests (#2581)
body:
newNamespaceRaceCatalog built its warehouse as "file://" + path. When two
subtests share a name, Go suffixes the second with "#01", and t.TempDir keeps
that '#' in the directory name, so the warehouse URI gained a fragment. View
locations then resolved outside the test's temp dir, and TestRenameView's
duplicate "db.child" subtests failed whenever a previous run had left that
stray directory behind.

Build the URI with url.URL so the path is escaped, and give the
TestRenameView subtests distinct names.

subject: test(catalog/sql): queue SQLite writers on a busy timeout in the shared test DSN (#2545)
body:
The two concurrent table/view collision tests and the ubuntu CI runners
still surfaced SQLITE_BUSY (database is locked) instead of the catalog
sentinels because the losing writer's retry budget ran out before the
winner committed, as seen in PR #2376's run 42457673447. Issue #1793
tracks the sibling sentinel test hitting the same error since August.

Put the busy timeout in the file-backed SQLite DSN the whole suite
shares, as the NewCatalog documentation already prescribes for callers
with concurrent writers: every pooled connection now waits for the
competing writer instead of erroring. sqliteshim selects mattn (cgo) or
modernc, whose DSN parameters differ, so branch on
sqliteshim.DriverName().

TestCreateNamespaceConcurrent already appended busy_timeout to the DSN
per kevinjqliu's analysis in #1793; it now inherits it from the shared
DSN instead.

Fixes #1793
